title: The Insurance Rule That Keeps Doomed Beach Houses Standing
summary:
Richard Foreman's house is stranded on the beach in Rodanthe, North Carolina. The stairs were ripped away by waves years ago, so there's no way in or out. The house sits 20 feet in the air on stilts meant to protect it from hurricane storm surge. But there haven't been any big storms recently — just the rising ocean slowly eating away the sand. Six years ago, it was a popular vacation rental called Sea 'n Delight. Today, it's uninhabitable. At high tide, the Atlantic runs beneath the entire house.

This is happening because of erosion, made worse by sea level rise caused by climate change. More than 30 homes have collapsed in Dare County since 2020. Four of Foreman's neighbors have fallen into the ocean in the last two years. The National Park Service, which manages the area as part of Cape Hatteras National Seashore, says more than 100 homes on North Carolina's barrier islands are at risk in the next decade. At least half a dozen are in imminent danger.

So why isn't anyone removing these houses? The answer involves what one expert calls "perverse incentives" created by FEMA, the Federal Emergency Management Agency. FEMA provides most residential flood insurance in the U.S. It pays homeowners after a house collapses — but not before. That means owners could lose tens or even hundreds of thousands of dollars by tearing down a doomed house early. "The homeowner is incentivized to wait for collapse and get a payout," says John Ryan-Henry, a policy analyst at the Coastal States Organization.

When homes collapse, they pollute the water and leave wreckage. "It leaves a legacy of hazard on the beach," says Lisa Sharrard, a longtime flood insurance agent. The Park Service collected more than 480 tons of home debris in 18 months. Foreman's house hasn't been emptied — couches, refrigerator, even steak knives are still inside. "If they would settle with me for the insurance, I would have it torn down tomorrow," he says. FEMA says it can't change the rules unless Congress amends the law. A bipartisan bill introduced in 2025 is stalled in the House.
why_it_matters: This story shows that insurance rules and laws — not just storms — decide what happens to coastlines, and today's teenagers will inherit both the rising sea and the bill for cleaning up what it swallows.

background_read: FEMA, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (the U.S. government agency that handles disasters and runs most flood insurance), was created in 1979, but its insurance program is older: the National Flood Insurance Program started in 1968 after private companies stopped selling flood coverage because it lost them money.

Rodanthe sits on the Outer Banks, a thin chain of barrier islands off North Carolina that naturally shift and roll toward the mainland as the sea rises — a process houses and roads can interrupt, leaving buildings out over open water.
Cape Hatteras National Seashore, established in 1953 as the country's first national seashore, protects roughly 70 miles of those islands and takes in villages like Rodanthe.

Because the federal government both insures the homes and manages the shoreline, it ends up paying for houses that its own park is being pushed against. Congress, not FEMA, writes the insurance program's rules, which is why the agency says it cannot act alone.

perspectives.description: Owners like Richard Foreman bought with FEMA-backed insurance because private companies will not cover flood risk. From their side, a payout after collapse is the only way to recover money they already spent — tearing the house down early means eating the loss themselves.

Collapsed homes dump septic waste, appliances, and debris into the surf, and the 480 tons collected so far show the cost. Critics argue the system effectively pays people to pollute and to leave hazardous wreckage on public beaches.

Analysts point out the odd arrangement: the government insures coastal homes while another government agency, the Park Service, manages the sand those homes are sliding into. The flood insurance program was designed decades ago, when sea level rise was not priced into the rules.

The bipartisan bill stalled in the House could let FEMA settle before a collapse and fund early demolition or buyouts. Whether it passes depends on who pays the difference — owners, taxpayers, or both.
